items.prompt: We stayed inside ___ it was raining.

options.why: Although shows a surprise. Staying in when it rains is no surprise.
Or gives a choice.
But shows a difference. Here we need a reason.

hints: Why did we stay inside?
You need a word that gives a reason.
Read the sentence aloud with each word.
items.explanation: Because gives the reason: we stayed inside because it was raining.

items.prompt: ___ it was late, Arif kept reading his book.

options.why: Being late is not a reason to keep reading.
So shows a result, and it does not start a sentence like this.
If does not fit, because it really was late.

hints: Is it surprising that Arif kept reading when it was late?
You need a word that shows a surprise or a contrast.
Try each word at the start and read the sentence aloud.
items.explanation: Although shows a contrast. It was late, but Arif kept reading anyway.

items.prompt:
Which part of the sentence can stand on its own?
When the bell rang, the children ran outside.

options.why: This leaves us asking: what happened when the bell rang?
This is only part of a clause.
This is not a clause on its own.

hints: A main clause makes sense on its own.
Read each part aloud. Does it sound finished?
Which part does not leave you waiting for more?
items.explanation: The children ran outside makes sense on its own, so it is the main clause. When the bell rang needs the rest of the sentence.

items.prompt: Match the beginnings to the best endings.
hints: Read the joining word at the start of each ending.
Until shows a time limit, while shows two things at once, and although shows a contrast.
Start with Sara hummed a song. Which ending shows something happening at the same time?
items.explanation: Each joining word has a job. If shows a condition, until shows a time limit and while shows two things at once. Because gives a reason, and although shows a contrast.

items.prompt: Which sentence joins the ideas correctly with although?

options.text: Although it was sunny it, was cold.
options.why: The comma goes after sunny.

options.text: It was sunny although, it was cold.
options.why: Do not put a comma straight after although.

options.text: Although, it was sunny it was cold.
options.why: Although starts the first clause, so there is no comma after it.

options.text: Although it was sunny, it was cold.

hints: The although part comes first here.
When the although clause comes first, put a comma at its end.
Find where the although clause ends and the main clause begins.
items.explanation: Although it was sunny is the first clause, so a comma goes after sunny, before the main clause.

items.prompt:
Where should the comma go?
If you finish early you can read a book.

options.text: If, you finish early you can read a book.
options.why: If starts the clause. There is no comma after it.

options.text: If you finish early, you can read a book.
If you finish, early you can read a book.
options.why: Early belongs with finish.

options.text: If you finish early you can, read a book.
options.why: Read a book belongs with can.

hints: The sentence starts with an if clause.
Find where the if clause ends.
The main clause is the part that could stand alone.
items.explanation: If you finish early is the first clause, so the comma goes after early. You can read a book is the main clause.

items.prompt: Sort the clauses. Can they stand alone?
hints: Read each clause aloud.
Does it sound finished, or does it leave you waiting?
Look at the first word of each clause. Is it a joining word?
items.explanation: Main clauses like the dog barked make sense alone. Clauses that start with because, when, although or if need a main clause.

items.prompt: You cannot go out to play ___ you tidy your room.

options.why: Tidying is not the reason you cannot play.
Although shows a contrast. It does not fit here.
So shows a result.

hints: What must happen before you can play?
You need a word that means if you do not.
Read the sentence with if you do not in the gap. Then find a one-word match.
items.explanation: Unless means if you do not. You cannot play unless you tidy your room.

items.prompt: Choose 2 sentences that are complex sentences.

options.why: This has only one clause.

options.text: We played outside after the rain stopped.
I like rice and I like noodles.
options.why: And joins two main clauses. That is a compound sentence.

options.text: While Dad cooked, we laid the table.

options.why: This is a one-word command.

hints: A complex sentence has a main clause and a clause that cannot stand alone.
Look for words like after, while, because and although.
Check that one part of the sentence would not make sense on its own.
items.explanation: After the rain stopped and while Dad cooked cannot stand alone. Each is joined to a main clause, so those sentences are complex.

items.prompt:
Choose while, until or because.
Keep stirring the soup ___ it starts to bubble.
hints: When should you stop stirring?
One of the words means up to the time when.
Try each word in the gap and read the sentence aloud.
items.explanation: Until means up to the time when. You stir the soup until it bubbles, and then you stop.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a complex sentence?

options.text: Since it was Sunday, the shops opened late.
It was Sunday and the shops opened late.
options.why: And joins two main clauses.
This is a simple sentence with one clause.

options.text: The shops opened late, the market was busy.
options.why: Two main clauses cannot be joined with just a comma.

hints: A complex sentence has a clause that cannot stand alone.
Look for a joining word at the start of a clause.
Which sentence has a clause that leaves you waiting for more?
items.explanation: Since it was Sunday cannot stand alone. It is joined to the main clause the shops opened late, so the sentence is complex.

items.prompt: In which sentence does since mean because?

options.why: Here since means from that time.

options.text: Since Monday, the shop has been closed.
options.why: Here since means from that day.

options.text: Since it was raining, we took the bus.
We have been friends since we were five.
options.why: Here since means from that time.

hints: Since can be about time or about reasons.
Try swapping since for because in each sentence.
Which sentence still makes sense with because?
items.explanation: In Since it was raining, we took the bus, since gives a reason, so it means because. In the others, since means from a time.

items.prompt:
Choose the best word.
I put on my coat ___ it was cold outside.
hints: The second part gives a reason.
Which word means for this reason?
Try each word in the sentence.
items.explanation: Because joins the reason (it was cold) to the action (I put on my coat).

items.prompt:
Which word starts the extra clause?
Dewi waited until the rain stopped.

options.why: Dewi is the subject of the main clause.
Waited is the main verb.
Stopped is the verb in the extra clause, but it does not start it.

hints: A clause often starts with a joining word.
The joining word tells how the two parts connect.
It is a word about time.
items.explanation: Until starts the extra clause: until the rain stopped.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to make a complex sentence.
items.answer: Although it was late, Hadi kept reading.
hints: The sentence starts with a joining word.
The first clause ends with a comma.
Although it was late is the first clause.
items.explanation: Although it was late is the extra clause. Hadi kept reading is the main clause.

items.prompt:
Write the word that joins the two clauses.
Citra can swim because she practises every day.
hints: Look for the word between the two ideas.
It gives a reason.
It comes after the first clause and before the second.
items.explanation: Because tells us the reason Citra can swim, so it joins the two clauses.

items.prompt: Match each beginning to the best ending.
pairs: as soon as everyone is here.
although she had slept for ten hours.
hints: Read each beginning and think what makes sense.
Look for the ending that gives a time, a reason or a surprise.
Although she had slept is a surprise about being tired.
items.explanation: Each ending adds an idea that fits: a time, a surprise, a reason or something happening at once.

items.prompt:
Where does the comma go?
Because the road was flooded the bus took another route.

options.text: Because, the road was flooded the bus took another route.
options.why: The comma should not split the joining word from the clause.

options.text: Because the road was flooded, the bus took another route.
Because the road was flooded the bus, took another route.
options.why: This splits the subject from its verb.

options.text: Because the road was flooded the bus took, another route.
options.why: This splits the verb from its object.

hints: Find where the first clause ends.
The extra clause comes first here.
Put the comma between the two clauses.
items.explanation: When the extra clause comes first, a comma goes between it and the main clause.

items.prompt:
Wulan sang while her mum cooked.
Which part is the subordinate clause?

options.why: This can stand on its own, so it is the main clause.
This is only part of a clause.
This cuts across both clauses.

hints: A subordinate clause cannot stand alone.
It starts with a joining word.
Look for the part that starts with while.
items.explanation: While her mum cooked cannot stand on its own, so it is the subordinate clause.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences. Are they complex sentences?

items.text: Tom ran because he was late.
Unless it rains, we will play.
I like rice but Ina likes noodles.
Although she was tired, she smiled.

hints: A complex sentence has a main clause and a clause that depends on it.
Look for joining words like because, unless and although.
And and but join equal parts instead.
items.explanation: Complex sentences use a joining word such as because, unless or although to attach an extra clause.

items.prompt:
Hadi wanted to buy the book. He did not have enough money.
Which sentence joins these ideas best?

options.text: Hadi wanted to buy the book because he did not have enough money.
options.why: Not having enough money is not a reason for wanting a book.

options.text: Hadi wanted to buy the book unless he did not have enough money.
options.why: Unless means if not, so it changes the meaning.

options.text: Hadi wanted to buy the book until he did not have enough money.
options.why: Until is about time, and does not fit.

options.text: Hadi wanted to buy the book although he did not have enough money.

hints: Think about how the two ideas connect.
They go against each other.
Which word shows a contrast, something unexpected?
items.explanation: Although shows a contrast: Hadi still wanted the book even though he had little money.

items.prompt:
Write the missing word. It means if not.
The plants will die ___ you water them.
hints: Read the clue: it means if not.
The plants will die if you do not water them.
The word starts with u.
items.explanation: Unless means if not, so the plants will die unless you water them.

items.prompt:
Choose the best word for each gap.
Maya will not go swimming ___ the water is warm enough. She will wait ___ her brother arrives.
hints: Read each sentence and think about what makes sense.
First gap: she will go only if the water is warm.
Second gap: waiting continues up to a moment in time.
items.explanation: Unless means if not, and until shows she waits up to the time her brother arrives.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT a complete sentence?

options.why: This is a complete sentence. It has a subject and a verb.

options.text: Although the bus was late, we arrived on time.
options.why: This is complete. The main clause is we arrived on time.

options.text: We waited because the bus was late.
options.why: This is complete. The main clause is we waited.

hints: A complete sentence needs a main clause.
A clause starting with although cannot stand alone.
Look for one that has only an extra clause.
items.explanation: Although the bus was late is only a subordinate clause. It needs a main clause to complete it.

items.prompt: Choose 2 sentences where the comma is in the correct place.

options.text: While Rina slept, the rain stopped.
The rain stopped while, Rina slept.
options.why: The comma splits the joining word from its clause.

options.text: If you are hungry, there is rice.
Unless, you hurry we will miss the show.
options.why: The comma should come after the whole clause, not after Unless.

options.text: Because it was hot we swam, in the lake.
options.why: The comma is in the middle of the main clause.

hints: A comma goes after an extra clause that comes first.
It does not split a joining word from its clause.
Check each sentence for the end of the first clause.
items.explanation: In both correct sentences, the extra clause comes first and a comma follows it.

items.prompt:
Ines was nervous. She still sang on stage.
Which sentence joins these ideas most clearly?

options.text: Ines was nervous, she still sang on stage.
options.why: Joining two sentences with only a comma is not enough.

options.text: Ines was nervous because she still sang on stage.
options.why: Singing is not the reason for being nervous.

options.text: Ines was nervous unless she still sang on stage.
options.why: Unless means if not, so the meaning is confused.

options.text: Although Ines was nervous, she still sang on stage.

hints: Ask how the two ideas relate.
She was nervous but sang anyway.
A joining word of contrast is needed, with a correct comma.
items.explanation: Although shows the contrast. The comma sits between the two clauses.

items.prompt: Which sentence has a subordinate clause that tells WHEN?

options.text: Leo packed his bag because the bell rang.
options.why: Because tells why, not when.

options.text: Leo packed his bag if the bell rang.
options.why: If gives a condition, not a time.

options.text: Leo packed his bag after the bell rang.
Leo packed his bag although the bell rang.
options.why: Although shows a contrast, not a time.

hints: When means at what time.
Which joining word links two moments?
Cross out why, if and contrast words.
items.explanation: After tells us when Leo packed his bag.

items.prompt: In which sentence does before join two clauses?

options.text: Kofi finished his homework before dinner.
options.why: Here before is followed by a noun, so it is a preposition.

options.text: Kofi finished his homework before dinner was ready.
Before school, Kofi fed the hens.
options.why: Here before is followed by a noun, so it is a preposition.
Here before ends the sentence and does not start a clause.

hints: A clause has a subject and a verb.
Look for the sentence where a subject and a verb follow before.
Dinner alone is only a noun.
items.explanation: In the second sentence, before is followed by dinner was ready, which has a subject and a verb. So it joins two clauses.

items.prompt:
Choose the 2 connectives in this sentence.
Although it was late, Ravi kept working because he wanted to finish.

options.why: Late is an adjective, not a connective.
Working is a verb, not a connective.
Finish is a verb, not a connective.

hints: A connective joins parts of a sentence.
Look for words that start extra clauses.
One is at the start of the sentence and one is in the middle.
items.explanation: Although and because join clauses, so they are connectives.

items.prompt: Sort the connectives by the job they do.
hints: Time connectives tell when.
Reason connectives tell why.
Contrast connectives show things that are different.
items.explanation: Before, until and after link time. Because and so that link reasons. Although and but show contrast.

items.prompt:
Copy the connective that joins the two clauses.
Dewi took an umbrella because the sky looked dark.
hints: A connective is a joining word.
It comes in the middle of the sentence.
It tells why Dewi took an umbrella.
items.explanation: Because joins the two clauses and gives the reason.

items.prompt: True or false: In the sentence "We stayed inside because it was raining", the word because joins two clauses.
hints: Find the word that links the clauses.
Because joins we stayed inside to it was raining.
Conjunctions join clauses.
items.explanation: Because is a conjunction that joins a main clause to a clause that gives the reason.

items.prompt: True or false: The word although is a noun.
hints: Can you touch an although?
It joins two ideas.
It is a joining word.
items.explanation: Although is a conjunction. It joins clauses, for example Although it was cold, we went out.

items.prompt: True or false: The sentence "Although it was cold, we went swimming" is a complex sentence.
hints: Find the main clause.
Find the clause that cannot stand alone.
It has two clauses joined by although.
items.explanation: A complex sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause. Although it was cold is the subordinate clause.

items.prompt: True or false: The word unless means the same as because.
hints: Try putting if not in its place.
Unless sets a condition.
It does not give a reason.
items.explanation: Unless means if not. Because gives a reason.

items.prompt: True or false: The sentence "We will go to the beach unless it rains" means we will go if it rains.
hints: Replace unless with if not.
What happens when it rains?
We will not go if it rains.
items.explanation: Unless means if not, so we will go to the beach only if it does not rain.

items.prompt: True or false: The word until is a conjunction in the sentence "Wait here until I come back".
hints: What does until link?
It joins two clauses.
Wait here is the main clause.
items.explanation: Until joins the main clause to a clause telling us when the waiting stops.
